findings.actualquote: component logs commonly go to journald on systemd hosts.
findings.why: The cited Logging Architecture page puts workload container logs under /var/log/pods by default, and on systemd it sends kubelet and container-runtime logs to journald by default. The same page says pod-hosted control-plane components write files under /var/log and do not write to the systemd journal. The sentence treats those classes as one common journald destination, next to the kubeadm static-Pod path.
findings.fix: Name kubelet and the container runtime for the systemd journald default, and say pod-hosted control-plane components log to files under /var/log rather than to journald.

claims.support_note: inode(7) stores owner, group, mode and timestamps; POSIX ls -l prints that metadata. Contents are the file data the inode describes.
Ubuntu file(1) classifies printable text separately from other data, which it describes as usually binary.
null(4) documents /dev/null as a special file created with mknod as a character device.
proc(5) defines /proc as a pseudo-filesystem of process and system information.
Path resolution walks directory components, and POSIX ls lists the names contained in a directory.
A pathname starting with / is absolute and starts at the process root, usually the filesystem root.
FHS calls /home an optional, commonly default placement. Apple says boot-volume homes live in /Users and network homes also exist, so commonly is the right strength.
FHS 3.0 defines /etc as host-specific system configuration. Often matches that convention, not every config file.
FHS defines /var/log as the directory for miscellaneous log files.
FHS says /tmp data may be deleted in a site-specific way and recommends boot cleanup without requiring it.
kubeadm writes control-plane static Pod manifests to /etc/kubernetes/manifests and kubelet watches that directory. Dry-run uses a temporary folder, which the page does not deny.
kubectl uses only --kubeconfig when set, otherwise $KUBECONFIG, and otherwise ${HOME}/.kube/config. By default matches that last case.
Kubelet directs the runtime to write container logs under /var/log/pods by default, and podLogsDir can change that path. Normally matches the default.
Journald-by-default is stated for kubelet and the container runtime on systemd. Pod-hosted control-plane components write files under /var/log and explicitly do not write to the journal.
An unquoted bare tilde-prefix with an empty login name expands to HOME.
POSIX pwd writes an absolute pathname of the current working directory.
With no operand, POSIX ls behaves as if the operand were dot, the current directory.
POSIX ls -l writes entry type, permission classes, link count, owner, group, size, modification time and name.
POSIX cd changes the shell working directory. It does not rename or move directory entries.
With HOME set, cd with no operand uses HOME. A bare unquoted ~ expands to HOME. Dot-dot is the parent component.
Bash converts cd - to $OLDPWD before the change. POSIX uses OLDPWD for the operand -. Both also write the new absolute path when it can be determined.
A pathname without a leading / starts at the current working directory, or at an openat directory fd. cd can also search CDPATH unless the operand starts with /.
Path resolution treats . as the directory itself and .. as its parent, and does not walk above /.
./script.sh is a relative pathname looked up in the current directory. A command name with no slash is found through function, builtin, then PATH search.
POSIX cat reads the named files in order and writes their bytes to standard output.
With no options, POSIX head acts as -n 10. -n selects a line count, and a shorter file is copied whole.
POSIX tail assumes -n 10 when -c, -n and -r are absent. -n 1 is the last line. GNU tail documents the same default and -n.
POSIX ls -l writes the entry's metadata. It does not write the file's contents.
The v1 Config type includes context names, usernames, cluster server addresses, client-certificate-data and bearer tokens. The kubectl page supplies the file-selection rule, not those fields.
Plain POSIX mkdir creates the named directory. Only -p creates missing intermediate components.
mkdir -p creates missing parents and succeeds when the named directories already exist.
POSIX touch creates a missing file and otherwise updates timestamps through utimensat. That update does not replace file data.
POSIX ls omits names beginning with a period unless -a or -A is set. -a writes those names. The rule is listing, not an access check.
The long-format mode is entry type, then three-character owner, group and other fields. d is directory and - is a regular file.
For ordinary files the three bits are read, write and execute. open(2) returns EACCES when the requested access is not allowed.
Path resolution names the first bit read permission. POSIX.1-2024 opendir fails with EACCES when read permission is denied on the directory, and readdir then reads its entries.
On a directory the third bit is search permission. Missing search on the current lookup directory returns EACCES.
Creating a file needs write on the parent, and unlink needs write on the containing directory. Both also require search on the path. Sticky-bit and other errors remain extra restrictions.
Owner mode or ACL_USER_OBJ is used when the effective UID is the owner. Group members who are not the owner are checked against the group class, not the owner bits.
Every non-final component needs search permission. ACLs can further restrict access, and CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE or CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH can bypass some checks.
CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE bypasses file read, write and execute checks, with the execute-bit caveat. CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH bypasses file read and directory read and search checks.
POSIX ls -d does not treat a directory operand differently from other file types, so it reports the directory entry rather than its children.
Bash > creates a missing target and truncates an existing one. With noclobber, > fails when the target is an existing regular file.
Single quotes preserve the literal value of every enclosed character. The ingredient strings contain no single quote.
The playground receipt recorded initial root and HOME=/root, then su - ubuntu reached the existing ubuntu account and /home/ubuntu. One image only.
As ubuntu, ls /root returned Permission denied status 2, and ls -ld /root showed root-owned drwx------. This is that host, not every system.
cd changes to a directory. Path resolution returns ENOTDIR, Not a directory, when a component used as a directory is neither a directory nor a symlink to one.

A missing component returns ENOENT, No such file or directory. Denied search or requested access returns EACCES, Permission denied. The page points toward those checks and does not say the message is exhaustive.
POSIX writes the new path when CDPATH supplies it or the operand is -. A no-option cd that does not use CDPATH has no required success message.
Components are substrings delimited by /. A leading / also marks an absolute pathname.
A one-line file is shorter than the default ten lines, so cat, head and tail each show that line. The receipt saw one ingredient line from each single-file read.
cat writes inputs in argument order. head -n 1 is the first line and tail -n 1 is the last. The receipt showed bread, then pasta, then coffee, with head and tail selecting the ends.
